title: Utilization of Dental Care Among Young American Indian Children From the Northern Plains
html:
ABSTRACT

Objectives

American Indian (AI) children have high rates of caries. This study described dental service utilization among AI children and examined relationships of social determinants of health (SDOH) with utilization and oral health.

Methods

This secondary data analysis used data extracted from a randomized controlled trial of a motivational interviewing (MI) intervention implemented to reduce dental decay in AI children aged 0–3 years (N = 535 parent–child dyads). Parents self-reported demographic, SDOH and child dental service utilization information. Utilization measures between 0 and 36 months of age included: (1) initiation of dental care by age 1 year, (2) fluoride varnish (FV) in the past year and (3) routine dental visit in the past year. Oral health was measured as decayed, missing and filled tooth surfaces (dmfs) from the 36-month dental evaluation. Regressions were estimated to examine the relationships of SDOH with utilization and dmfs.

Results

Dental care was initiated by age 1 for 34% of children. At 24 and 36 months, 47% and 58% of children, respectively, received FV in the past year. At these ages, 29% and 46% of children, respectively, had ≥ 1 routine visits in the past year. Access to a working vehicle (OR = 1.79; CI: 1.04, 3.07), shorter travel times to closest dental clinic (OR = 0.49; CI: 0.31, 0.78) and stronger health literacy (OR = 1.46; CI: 1.11, 1.93) were associated with routine visits. Higher income was negatively associated with dmfs (RR = 0.32; CI: 0.17, 0.58). Participation in the MI intervention was associated with receiving FV (OR = 1.45; CI: 1.03, 2.04).

Conclusions

Many children did not receive recommended dental care. Specific SDOH were associated with service utilization.
